I/O instructions allow you to perform operations with the input and output ports of a PLC.
Interrupts are also associated with I/O devices, and there are special instructions that allow you to control the operation of interrupts.
We will look at the operation and usage of interrupts. By understanding the operation and usage, you will find it easy to comprehend the instructions for controlling interrupts.
Let's begin the lesson on I/O AND INTERRUPT INSTRUCTIONS..................
LESSON MENU
I/O AND INTERRUPT INSTRUCTIONS
I/O and interrupt instructions allow you to control and monitor the inputs, outputs, and status of modules attached to a PLC. These modules provide the connection of the PLC to the outside world.
DISCUSSION

For example, a PLC may be used to monitor the number of items that pass by a sensor on four different stages of an assembly line. In this case, the PLC requires four inputs from sensors to the PLC itself...
An input module can be used to attach to the PLC, normally in a slot. The sensors are then attached to the PLC module, which is monitored by the PLC. The module is an input device.

There are hundreds of different modules providing many different types of external connections; however, the ladder logic programs appear the same. All inputs and outputs are read as individual bits or groups of bits...
The list below shows the I/O instructions. Let's look at each of these instructions and the parameters they require for operation.
This is the Immediate Input with Mask (IIM) instruction. This instruction is used to get the current values of the input module and place them in their associated data file in memory.

When a PLC ladder logic program is running, input data is not constantly being read into a data file in memory. Instead, the PLC scans all inputs at the same time and sets all outputs at the same time before continuing...
After it has read all inputs and set all outputs, the ladder is evaluated again. Once the end of the ladder is reached, the process starts again.

If you have a very long ladder logic program, you may not want to wait a complete cycle for the input value to change. This is where the IIM instruction is used. When this instruction is called, the particular input you specify is immediately scanned...
After the input is scanned and the associated data is set in the data file, the processor continues in the ladder logic that follows the IIM instruction.
All of the instructions after the IIM instruction will have the new information in the data file that was just scanned in.

The IIM instruction requires two parameters: a slot and a mask. Slot is a term that refers to identifying whether you are addressing the input or output section of the module and the slot number position as well as the word within it. The mask is a process that allows you to specify the bits you want to scan of the word identified in the slot.....
I : 0 Input Module 0 Word 0 FF (11111111)
I : 2.2 Input Module 2 Word 2 A5 (10100101)
I : 3 Input Module 3 Word 3 F0 (11110000))

You do not have to input the entire data set of the input device. For example, let's look at an input that has 8 bits. Bits 0 through 3 are attached to the sensors we mentioned earlier, and 4 through 7 are attached to sensors that indicate if the assembly line is active...

Since our process will look at the number of items that pass sensors at each point in a process, it is critical to know when an item passes by. In this case, we elect to add extra input scans only for the items that pass sensor bits in the data file...

To do this, we use the mask "11110000". The ones specify the inputs associated with these bits that we want read and stored in the data file. The zeros indicate which bits should remain unchanged......
The actual instruction, however, does not take 11110000 as a valid mask. Instead, this binary value must be converted to hexadecimal. The equivalent hexadecimal value for 11110000 is F0...

Also, a data register in the PLC memory can be specified for the mask. The instruction looks in that register to get the mask. Using this method allows you to change the mask whenever you want during execution of the ladder logic code...

Remember, when using IIM instruction, be sure to write your ladder logic properly, accounting for the fact that the data file can change during the ladder logic evaluation and not just during the initial input scan...

The next instruction we will look at is the Immediate Output with Mask (IOM) instruction. This instruction is similar to the IIM instruction, with the exception that it works with the output modules instead of the input modules...

This instruction, when called, takes the bits of a data file for an output slot and sends those bit values to that output module. This is also used within a ladder logic program when the output needs to be set before the normal output set...

The IOM instruction takes the same parameters as the IIM instruction, slot with word and mask. Again, ones in the mask change the output bit settings and zeroes cause those particular output bits to remain unchanged...
I : 0 Input Module 0 Word 0 IF (00011111)
I : 3 Input Module 3 Word 0 00 (00000000)
I : 2.2 Input Module 2 Word 2 11 (00010001))-

The last I/O instruction we will examine is the I/O Refresh (REF) instruction. This instruction, when used, writes all outputs, services the communications, and reads all inputs of the modules, in that order...
This instruction doesn't use parameters, so masks cannot be used. Just as with IIM and IOM, the PLC continues with the new data that follows the REF instruction.
Now we will discuss the interrupt instructions used by I/O in a PLC system. Before we look at these instructions, however, let's look at what an interrupt is.
An interrupt is used to pause the PLC and do something else. An input device can be set so that when a particular condition occurs on its inputs, it sends an interrupt to the PLC.

The interrupt signal sent to the PLC finishes the current operation and then goes to a subroutine associated with the interrupt. The PLC evaluates this subroutine ladder logic and then returns to where it had left off in its normal operation...
Interrupts are used where it is critical for the PLC to perform some action when a certain condition arises at an I/O device.
The first two instructions are the I/O Interrupt Disable (IID) and I/O Interrupt Enable (IIE) instructions. These instructions are normally used together.

There may be portions of your ladder logic code that you don't want interrupted. This is especially true for subroutines or main ladder logic that is time critical. In that case, you want to temporarily ignore specific interrupts...

To disable interrupts from I/O modules, you use the IID (I/O Interrupt Disable) instruction. This instruction requires you to specify which slot or slots to disable. Below are examples of how you can specify these types of instructions...
To enable the interrupts again, use the IIE (I/O Interrupt Enable) instruction, again providing the slots to enable.

Remember, if an interrupt is disabled, the PLC will not know if that interrupt occurs. If you have very important interrupts, make sure they are enabled again as soon as you no longer need them disabled.......................
The next instruction is the Reset Pending I/O Interrupt (RPI) instruction. This instruction is used when an I/O module sends an interrupt to the PLC.
The instruction resets the interrupt request of the I/O module and indicates to the I/O module that the interrupt request has been aborted. This instruction also requires a list of slots to reset.
In more general terms, this instruction tells an I/O module or modules that the PLC recognizes the interrupt requests but is going to ignore them, and it resets the requests.

We have examined the I/O and Interrupt instruction of a PLC. In the experiment, you will see the operation of an example of these types of instructions.
This completes the information on I/O AND INTERRUPT INSTRUCTIONS.

1. The Immediate Input with Mask (IIM) instruction is used to update the input data files at once instead of waiting for the normal input scan. You can specify with a mask what input bits you want to scan at once.

2. The Immediate Output with Mask (IOM) instruction is used to update the output data files at once instead of waiting for the normal output set. Again, you can specify with a mask what output bits you want to set..

3. The I/O Refresh (REF) instruction is used to set all outputs, perform communication operations, and scan all inputs at once instead of waiting for the normal output, communications, and input scan. This instruction does not use masks.
4. The I/O Interrupt Disable and Enable (IID and IIE) are used to disable and enable the PLC from seeing interrupts from the different IO modules.
5. The Reset Pending I/O Interrupt (RPI) is used to abort an interrupt that has been set on any of the specified modules to the instruction.

The program shown below is the ladder logic program you are going to enter to demonstrate some of the I/O and interrupt instructions that you learned in the first part of this lesson.
Before we actually begin entering the program into the PLC APS software, let's look at what the program should do. This will help us understand if the program is operating properly when we test it...

It is important to realize that the Immediate Input with Mask and Immediate Output with Mask instructions are normally used in large ladder logic programs where timing is critical and one can't wait until the end of the cycle to write or scan inputs and outputs...

For this reason, the program you enter will not allow you to see the overall benefits to the IIM or IOM instructions. The purpose of this experiment is to let you see how they are entered into ladder logic...

Remember, at the beginning of the ladder logic program, the PLC will have just finished writing the outputs, performing communication operations, and scanning the inputs. For this reason, we know the inputs and outputs are up to date...
The first rung checks to see if the START button on the 5050-1 card is pressed down. Remember, the START button is connected to the 0 input of the input modules built into the PLC.

When the switch is pressed in, the associated bit in the input data file is set to one when scanned by the PLC. If the key is not being pressed, the bit will be scanned and indicated by a zero in the data file.e...

In this rung, the LED attached to output 0 of the output module will be enabled if the START switch is pressed down. When the button is released and this rung is evaluated again, the LED will extinguish..

Rung 2 contains the Immediate Output with Mask instruction. The parameters to this instruction indicate that we want to update all the output bits of output module 0, word 0. Remember, FFFF in hex is 1111111111111111 in binary. Ones indicate update with new values.
If the START button is pressed down, this instruction will cause the LED to illuminate now instead of at the normal output write cycle.

The next instruction is the Immediate Input with Mask. At this point, we want to scan the inputs again to see if any of the key conditions have changed. We are using a mask of FFFF so all inputs are updated.

The last rung checks to see if the STOP button is being pressed. This button is attached to the 1 input of the PLC inputs. While this button is pressed, the associated bit in the input data file is set to one.e...

With this bit set to one, the LED attached to output 1 of the output module will be enabled. Again, we don't need another IOM or IIM after this instruction because we are at the end of the ladder. The inputs and outputs will update before evaluation begins at the top of the ladder again...
It is very important to realize that these instructions are used in much larger programs where waiting until the end of the cycle before updating the outputs or scanning the inputs is not possible...
